findings.reason: The protected Python solution converts nodes into a hash set for O(1) membership and runs a postorder DFS traversal. If the current node is in targets or None, it returns node immediately. If both left and right child searches return non-None nodes, current node is the LCA; otherwise it bubbles up whichever child returned non-None. The solution runs in O(N + K) time and O(H + K) auxiliary space, which is concise and optimal; no candidate is required.

Postorder traversal inspects subtrees from bottom to top. Returning a target node immediately when found correctly short-circuits deeper traversal in its subtree because no proper descendant can be an ancestor of that target node. When left and right subtrees both return non-None targets, the current node is the lowest common meeting point for those targets.

Converting nodes to a set takes O(K) time and space. Postorder DFS visits each of N tree nodes at most once, using O(H) call stack space. Overall time is O(N + K) and auxiliary space is O(H + K). Complexity evidence is inherited and hash-bound.
Accepts root and nodes list, handles single target, ancestor targets, and targets spread across root subtrees, returning the exact TreeNode object representing the lowest common ancestor.

The approach accurately details target set lookup optimization, postorder DFS bubble-up logic, and O(N + K) time / O(H + K) space bounds. Alternatives and edge cases cover root-to-target path intersections, parent map walks, single targets, ancestor targets, and root-level target splits.

App Python and native Python solutions both execute the exact same postorder DFS with set membership checking, with SHA-256 digests 7464cf07ed6f1d2b573932951c870e676af6d762f504fe3ed9c2e3e7e597eb37 and 337873710262963ffb08dd4c5fc30cce973f11d7920a5c53732c64a61e091c9f.
